```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
set.seed(1)
library(timesift)
if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("TIMESIFT_DOCS_CACHE"))) source(Sys.getenv("TIMESIFT_DOCS_CACHE"))
has_torch <- requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) && torch::torch_is_installed()
```

A *learner* specifies how to fit a model and make predictions. `timesift` includes fifteen learners, including regression models, decision trees and neural networks. Each learner can be fitted using different summaries of a sensor record, such as weekly or monthly means. A model paired with one such summary is a *candidate*.

This article covers the available learners, compatible inputs, model settings, neural-network training and tuning. It also shows how to add a custom learner, response type or metric, and compares fitting times on a small example.

The examples use 150 sampling units, each measured every six hours for a year, and four responses recording presence or absence. The simulated responses depend on changes in each unit's readings across several weeks. Summarising over longer periods can remove those changes. The time scale of each summary is called its *grain*.

## Installation

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Install from CRAN
install.packages("timesift")

# Or install the development version from GitHub
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/timesift")
```

```bash
# Install from PyPI
pip install timesift

# with the torch encoders, the contrasts and the plots
pip install "timesift[torch,contrasts,plot]"

# Or install the development version from GitHub
pip install git+https://github.com/gcol33/timesift
```
:::

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r data}
sim <- simulate_records(n = 150L, mechanism = "lag", variables = 4L, days = 365L,
                        step_hours = 6, prevalence = 0.3, auc = 0.85, seed = 4L)
targets <- data.frame(unit = rownames(sim$y), sim$y)
colSums(sim$y)
```

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import timesift as ts

sim = ts.simulate_records(n=150, mechanism="lag", variables=4, days=365, step_hours=6,
                          prevalence=0.3, auc=0.85, seed=4)
y = sim.y
targets = pd.DataFrame({"unit": y.units, **dict(zip(y.variables, y.values.T.astype(int)))})
targets.drop(columns="unit").sum()
#> v01    48
#> v02    50
#> v03    44
#> v04    48
#> dtype: int64
```
:::

## One interface

::: {.lang-r-only}
A learner is a list containing `fit` and `predict` functions, its supported input types, whether it models responses jointly or separately, and its package requirements. Printing it shows these declarations and its settings. A setting shown as `NULL` takes its default when the model is fitted.
:::

::: {.lang-py-only}
A learner is an object holding `fit` and `predict` functions, its supported input types, whether it models responses jointly or separately, and its package requirements. Printing it shows these declarations and its settings. A setting shown as `None` takes its default when the model is fitted.
:::

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r print}
elasticnet()
forest(balance = TRUE)
```

```python
ts.elasticnet()
#> <timesift learner> elasticnet
#> reads   : tabular ; one model per response: yes, separate
#> data    : every representation of the run
#> settings: alpha = 0.5, n_inner = 10, squares = True, s = lambda.1se, n_lambda = 100, tol = 1e-08, threads = 1, seed = 1
ts.forest(balance=True)
#> <timesift learner> forest
#> reads   : tabular ; one model per response: yes, separate
#> data    : every representation of the run
#> settings: trees = None, mtry = None, min_node = None, balance = True, preset = default, seed = 1, threads = 1
```
:::

`fit` receives a numeric array indexed by `[unit, bin, channel]` and a response matrix with the same units. A bin is one time interval; a channel contains one variable and summary statistic, such as mean temperature. `predict` returns one column per response. Each learner receives the full response matrix, including learners that fit a separate model for each response.

::: {.lang-r-only}
`c()` binds learners into a set, which `timesift()` takes as `learners`.
:::

::: {.lang-py-only}
A list binds learners into a set, which `timesift()` takes as `learners`.
:::

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r set}
c(elasticnet(), forest(), cnn())
```

```python
print(*[ts.elasticnet(), ts.forest(), ts.cnn()], sep="\n\n")
#> <timesift learner> elasticnet
#> reads   : tabular ; one model per response: yes, separate
#> data    : every representation of the run
#> settings: alpha = 0.5, n_inner = 10, squares = True, s = lambda.1se, n_lambda = 100, tol = 1e-08, threads = 1, seed = 1
#>
#> <timesift learner> forest
#> reads   : tabular ; one model per response: yes, separate
#> data    : every representation of the run
#> settings: trees = None, mtry = None, min_node = None, balance = False, preset = default, seed = 1, threads = 1
#>
#> <timesift learner> cnn
#> reads   : sequence ; one model per response: no, joint
#> data    : every representation of the run
#> settings: channels = 16/32/64/128, kernel = 7, dropout = 0.3
#> needs   : torch
```
:::

## The learners that ship

Every shipped learner is registered under its own name, and its declarations can be read off the
constructor:

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r catalogue}
shipped <- learners()
built <- lapply(shipped, function(nm) getExportedValue("timesift", nm)())
data.frame(learner = shipped,
           reads = vapply(built, `[[`, "", "reads"),
           multi = vapply(built, `[[`, "", "multi"),
           needs = vapply(built, function(l) paste(l$needs, collapse = ", "), ""))
```

```python
built = [ts.get_learner(name) for name in ts.learners()]
pd.DataFrame({"learner": ts.learners(),
              "reads": [l.reads for l in built],
              "multi": [l.multi for l in built],
              "needs": [", ".join(l.needs) for l in built]})
#>          learner     reads     multi  needs
#> 0       additive   tabular  separate
#> 1       boosting   tabular  separate
#> 2            cnn  sequence     joint  torch
#> 3   discriminant   tabular  separate
#> 4     elasticnet   tabular  separate
#> 5       envelope   tabular  separate
#> 6         forest   tabular  separate
#> 7   hierarchical   tabular  separate
#> 8         linear   tabular  separate
#> 9           mars   tabular  separate
#> 10        maxent   tabular  separate
#> 11           mlp   tabular     joint  torch
#> 12    perceptron   tabular  separate
#> 13        rescnn  sequence     joint  torch
#> 14          tree   tabular  separate
```
:::

Twelve learners use a table of predictors and fit one model per response. The neural networks `mlp()`, `cnn()` and `rescnn()` fit all responses together, sharing internal features between responses. `mlp()` uses a table; `cnn()` and `rescnn()` use the time order of the bins. These three networks require torch. The other learners use the compiled implementation shared by the R and Python packages.

Each compiled learner is written from the published method and is checked in the test fixtures
against the package whose numbers it reproduces. The [biomod2 article](biomod2.html) maps each of
them to the biomod2 algorithm it corresponds to, with the option sets biomod2 uses.

| learner | model | numbers checked against | responses |
|---|---|---|---|
| `elasticnet()` | elastic net over every column and its square, penalty chosen by inner cross-validation | glmnet | every head |
| `linear()` | generalised linear model, terms searched by AIC | MASS `stepAIC()`, `glm()` | every head |
| `tree()` | classification and regression tree, pruned by inner cross-validation | rpart | every head |
| `forest()` | random forest | randomForest | every head |
| `boosting()` | gradient boosted trees, first or second order | gbm, xgboost | every head |
| `maxent()` | maximum entropy over maxnet's feature classes | maxnet | presence-absence |
| `envelope()` | surface range envelope | biomod2 `bm_SRE()` | presence-absence |
| `mars()` | multivariate adaptive regression splines | earth | every head |
| `discriminant()` | flexible discriminant analysis on a MARS basis | mda `fda(method = mars)` | presence-absence |
| `additive()` | additive model of thin plate regression splines | mgcv `gam(method = "GCV.Cp")` | every head |
| `perceptron()` | network of one hidden layer, fitted by BFGS | nnet | every head |
| `hierarchical()` | Bayesian logistic model, optional unit intercepts and spatial field | none | presence-absence |
| `mlp()` | fully connected encoder, joint head | torch | every head |
| `cnn()` | convolutional encoder, joint head | torch | every head |
| `rescnn()` | dilated residual convolutional encoder, joint head | torch | every head |

A *response head* specifies the type of values being predicted and the loss function used to fit them. "All response types" in the table means logistic fitting for presence-absence, squared-error fitting for continuous, abundance and ordinal responses, and Poisson fitting for counts. `hierarchical()` supports presence-absence. It approximates the posterior distribution using Laplace's method and integrates over a grid of hyperparameter values (Rue, Martino and Chopin 2009). Its `"nngp"` and `"hsgp"` options model spatial variation using coordinates supplied through `timesift(coords = )`.

## What a learner may be handed

A tabular learner reads the bins as a block of predictors, one column per bin of each channel.
Given `native()`, the record unreduced, it would be handed one column per reading, so the pair is
refused. When the learner is pinned to `native()` through `data =`, the refusal comes before the
record is read:

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r refuse-native, error = TRUE}
timesift(targets, sim$readings, y = starts_with("v"), id = unit, time = time,
         learners = forest(data = native()), verbose = FALSE)
```

```{.python error=true}
ts.timesift(targets, sim.readings, y="v*", id="unit", time="time",
            learners=ts.forest(data=ts.native()), verbose=False)
#> ValueError: forest() reads a tabular representation; native gives it one column per reading. Use grain(), multigrain() or lookback().
```
:::

Inside a `sift` the same pair is skipped and the run goes on. The candidate table keeps the skipped
pair, with the reason in `note`.

```{r skip-native}
mixed <- timesift(targets, sim$readings, y = starts_with("v"), id = unit, time = time,
                  learners = c(elasticnet(), forest()),
                  sift = c(native(), grain("month")),
                  resampling = cv(v = 5), n_inner = NULL, ensemble = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
mixed$candidates[c("candidate", "bins", "status")]
```


The native representation of this record has 1460 bins, one per reading. A sequence learner is
refused the opposite case: a representation that gives one row of features, such as
`multigrain()`, or one whose record turns out to hold a single bin. That refusal is shown with the
encoders below.

## Several learners in one run

`learners` takes a set or a named list. Names distinguish candidates that use different settings of the same learner. Each learner is fitted at every compatible grain in `sift`, unless its `data` argument specifies one representation. Here `linear()` uses monthly summaries. The elastic net uses a looser stopping tolerance to shorten the example; the settings section explains that choice.

Cross-validation divides the units into groups called *folds*. Each fold is predicted using models trained on the other folds. An additional split within the training data, called *inner cross-validation*, chooses candidates and estimates ensemble weights before the outer test fold is predicted. A response in one fold is called a *cell* in the scoring output. The score used here is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), which measures how well predictions rank presences above absences.

::: {.lang-py-only}
In Python `learners` takes a list, and a candidate reports under its learner's `name`, which `dataclasses.replace(learner, name="...")` sets.
:::

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r run}
models <- list(
  elasticnet = elasticnet(tol = 1e-4),
  linear = linear(data = grain("month")),
  tree = tree(),
  forest = forest(),
  forest_balanced = forest(balance = TRUE),
  gbm = boosting(),
  xgboost = boosting(method = "xgboost"),
  maxent = maxent()
)
run_time <- system.time(
  fit <- timesift(targets, sim$readings, y = starts_with("v"), id = unit, time = time,
                  learners = models, sift = grains("week", "month"),
                  resampling = cv(v = 5), n_inner = 3L, verbose = FALSE)
)
run_time[["elapsed"]]
```

```python
import time
from dataclasses import replace

models = [
    ts.elasticnet(tol=1e-4),
    ts.linear(data=ts.grain("month")),
    ts.tree(),
    ts.forest(),
    replace(ts.forest(balance=True), name="forest_balanced"),
    replace(ts.boosting(), name="gbm"),
    replace(ts.boosting(method="xgboost"), name="xgboost"),
    ts.maxent(),
]
start = time.perf_counter()
fit = ts.timesift(targets, sim.readings, y="v*", id="unit", time="time",
                  learners=models, sift=ts.grains("week", "month"),
                  resampling=ts.cv(v=5), n_inner=3, verbose=False)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
round(elapsed)
#> 26
```
:::

The run took [`r round(run_time[["elapsed"]])`]{.lang-r-only}[26]{.lang-py-only py="round(elapsed)"} seconds for 15 candidates. With three inner folds in
each of five outer folds, every candidate is fitted 5 x (3 + 1) = 20 times, three inner fits and
one outer fit in each outer fold, and once more on every target.

`summary()` lists the candidates in order of their mean score on the outer folds, with the number of
responses on which each scored highest, and then the held-out score of the procedure that chooses
and weights them.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

```python
print(ts.summary(fit))
#> timesift  150 targets, 4 responses, 5-fold random CV, roc_auc
#>
#> candidates, scored on the outer folds
#> candidate                         mean    won  responses
#> tree / month                     0.513      0  separate
#> xgboost / month                  0.549      0  separate
#> forest_balanced / month          0.560      0  separate
#> forest / month                   0.561      0  separate
#> elasticnet / month               0.583      0  separate
#> gbm / month                      0.589      0  separate
#> linear / month                   0.603      0  separate
#> tree / week                      0.623      0  separate
#> maxent / month                   0.624      0  separate
#> forest_balanced / week           0.638      0  separate
#> forest / week                    0.649      0  separate
#> gbm / week                       0.677      0  separate
#> xgboost / week                   0.697      0  separate
#> maxent / week                    0.779      2  separate
#> elasticnet / week                0.791      2  separate
#>
#> procedure, chosen and weighted inside each outer training fold
#> selected                         0.777  se 0.030
#> ensemble                         0.775  se 0.027
#> selected maxent / week in 4, elasticnet / week in 1 of 5 folds
#>
#> choice on every target  elasticnet / week
#> weights on every target  maxent / week 0.87   xgboost / week 0.05   elasticnet / week 0.04   linear / month 0.03   xgboost / month 0.01
```
:::

Each learner run at both grains scores higher at the weekly one, which is the grain the simulation
acts at. At the monthly grain the tree, both forests and gbm score [below 0.5, so they find nothing
there]{.lang-r-only}[between ]{.lang-py-only}[0.513]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % min(r['mean'] for r in ts.candidate_table(fit) if r['candidate'] in ('tree / month', 'forest / month', 'forest_balanced / month', 'gbm / month'))"}[ and ]{.lang-py-only}[0.589]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % max(r['mean'] for r in ts.candidate_table(fit) if r['candidate'] in ('tree / month', 'forest / month', 'forest_balanced / month', 'gbm / month'))"}. [`maxent / week`]{.lang-r-only}[`elasticnet / week`]{.lang-py-only py="'`' + ts.candidate_table(fit)[-1]['candidate'] + '`'"} has the highest mean, [0.750]{.lang-r-only}[0.791]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % ts.candidate_table(fit)[-1]['mean']"}, and scored highest on [all four]{.lang-r-only}[2 of the four]{.lang-py-only py="str(ts.candidate_table(fit)[-1]['won']) + ' of the four'"} responses. The procedure rows are the scores to report: inside each outer training fold the
inner folds chose a candidate and fitted the stack's weights, and the outer test fold then scored
that choice once, [0.741]{.lang-r-only}[0.777]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % ts.procedure_table(fit)[0]['mean']"} for the selected candidate and [0.740]{.lang-r-only}[0.775]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % ts.procedure_table(fit)[1]['mean']"} for the stack. The highest candidate
mean was picked out on the same folds it is scored on.

The candidate table records how each candidate was built: its learner, its grain, the number of
bins and channels, whether it was fitted, and, for a tuned learner, the settings it chose.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r candidates}
head(fit$candidates[c("candidate", "learner", "grain", "bins", "status")], 4)
```

```python
pd.DataFrame(fit.candidates)[["candidate", "learner", "grain", "bins"]].head(4)
#>             candidate     learner  grain  bins
#> 0   elasticnet / week  elasticnet   week    53
#> 1  elasticnet / month  elasticnet  month    12
#> 2      linear / month      linear  month    12
#> 3         tree / week        tree   week    53
```
:::

## One learner on one array

`fit_learner()` fits a learner to an array from `grain_matrix()` without the folds and the scoring
around it, and `predict()` on the result takes an array of the same bins and channels. The units
below are split in half once. The two arrays are built from the two halves of the record, over the
same calendar weeks.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r one-array}
train <- rownames(sim$y)[1:75]
test <- rownames(sim$y)[76:150]
in_train <- sim$readings$unit %in% train
week_train <- grain_matrix(sim$readings[in_train, ], unit, time, reading, grain = "week")
week_test <- grain_matrix(sim$readings[!in_train, ], unit, time, reading, grain = "week")
f <- fit_learner(elasticnet(), week_train, sim$y[train, ])
f
f$model[c("unfitted", "stopped")]
```

```python
train, test = y.take_units(np.arange(75)), y.take_units(np.arange(75, 150))
in_train = np.isin(sim.readings["unit"], train.units)

def rows(mask):
    return {k: v[mask] for k, v in sim.readings.items()}

week_train = ts.grain_matrix(rows(in_train), "unit", "time", "reading", grain="week")
week_test = ts.grain_matrix(rows(~in_train), "unit", "time", "reading", grain="week")
f = ts.fit_learner(ts.elasticnet(), week_train, train)
f.learner
#> <timesift learner> elasticnet
#> reads   : tabular ; one model per response: yes, separate
#> data    : every representation of the run
#> settings: alpha = 0.5, n_inner = 10, squares = True, s = lambda.1se, n_lambda = 100, tol = 1e-08, threads = 1, seed = 1
{k: f.model[k] for k in ("unfitted", "stopped")}
#> {'unfitted': [], 'stopped': []}
```
:::

`unfitted` lists responses with too few presences for penalty selection; their predictions use the prevalence in the training data. `stopped` lists responses whose penalty path ended early. Neither occurs here. Prediction requires the same bins used during fitting:

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r one-array-refuse, error = TRUE}
month_train <- grain_matrix(sim$readings[in_train, ], unit, time, reading, grain = "month")
month_test <- grain_matrix(sim$readings[!in_train, ], unit, time, reading, grain = "month")
predict(f, month_test)
```

```{.python error=true}
month_train = ts.grain_matrix(rows(in_train), "unit", "time", "reading", grain="month")
month_test = ts.grain_matrix(rows(~in_train), "unit", "time", "reading", grain="month")
f.predict(month_test)
#> ValueError: the representation predicted on has different channels or bins from the fitted one: 12 bins here and 53 bins in the fit. A calendar grain is read by its bins' instants, so a fit predicts a record over the same period; a lookback reads a span relative to each target and predicts any period.
```
:::

## Settings of the main learners

The settings below are the ones most often changed; each constructor's documentation lists the rest.

`elasticnet()` fits one penalised model per response over every column and, with `squares = TRUE`,
its square. `alpha` mixes the two penalties, `1` being the lasso and `0` ridge. `s` is where the
penalty path is read: `"lambda.1se"`, the largest penalty within one standard error of the least
held-out deviance, is glmnet's default, `"lambda.min"` is the penalty of least deviance, and a
number is a penalty given directly. `tol` is where the coordinate descent stops; the default leaves
the fit as close to the optimum as glmnet's own default does, and a looser one is faster.

`forest()` grows 500 trees by default, with `mtry` the square root of the column count under
presence-absence. `balance = TRUE` draws as many units of each class into every tree as the smaller
class holds, so a rare response's presences are half of each tree's draw. `boosting()` fits gbm's
first-order trees by default and XGBoost's second-order trees with `method = "xgboost"`, whose
`lambda` and `gamma` are the penalty on a leaf and the least gain a split must make. `maxent()`
builds maxnet's feature classes, the letters of `classes`: `l` linear, `q` quadratic, `p` pairwise
products, `h` hinges and `t` thresholds. Left `NULL`, the classes follow each response's presence
count, as maxnet chooses them.

The function below fits a learner on the training half and returns its AUC on the other half,
averaged over the four responses.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r settings}
held_out_auc <- function(l) {
  f <- fit_learner(l, week_train, sim$y[train, ])
  p <- predict(f, week_test)
  mean(vapply(colnames(p), function(v) roc_auc(sim$y[test, v], p[, v]), numeric(1)))
}
variants <- list(
  `elasticnet()` = elasticnet(),
  `elasticnet(s = "lambda.min")` = elasticnet(s = "lambda.min"),
  `elasticnet(alpha = 1)` = elasticnet(alpha = 1),
  `elasticnet(tol = 1e-4)` = elasticnet(tol = 1e-4),
  `forest()` = forest(),
  `forest(balance = TRUE)` = forest(balance = TRUE),
  `boosting()` = boosting(),
  `boosting(method = "xgboost")` = boosting(method = "xgboost"),
  `maxent()` = maxent(),
  `maxent(classes = "lq")` = maxent(classes = "lq")
)
round(vapply(variants, held_out_auc, numeric(1)), 3)
```

```python
def held_out_auc(learner):
    p = ts.fit_learner(learner, week_train, train).predict(week_test)
    return np.mean([ts.roc_auc(test.values[:, j], p[:, j]) for j in range(p.shape[1])])

variants = {
    "elasticnet()": ts.elasticnet(),
    'elasticnet(s="lambda.min")': ts.elasticnet(s="lambda.min"),
    "elasticnet(alpha=1)": ts.elasticnet(alpha=1),
    "elasticnet(tol=1e-4)": ts.elasticnet(tol=1e-4),
    "forest()": ts.forest(),
    "forest(balance=True)": ts.forest(balance=True),
    "boosting()": ts.boosting(),
    'boosting(method="xgboost")': ts.boosting(method="xgboost"),
    "maxent()": ts.maxent(),
    'maxent(classes="lq")': ts.maxent(classes="lq"),
}
held_out = pd.Series({name: held_out_auc(l) for name, l in variants.items()})
held_out.round(3)
#> elasticnet()                  0.729
#> elasticnet(s="lambda.min")    0.726
#> elasticnet(alpha=1)           0.727
#> elasticnet(tol=1e-4)          0.727
#> forest()                      0.626
#> forest(balance=True)          0.605
#> boosting()                    0.615
#> boosting(method="xgboost")    0.638
#> maxent()                      0.710
#> maxent(classes="lq")          0.736
#> dtype: float64
```
:::

On this split the elastic net read at `"lambda.min"` scores [0.680]{.lang-r-only}[0.726]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[1]"} against [0.631]{.lang-r-only}[0.729]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[0]"} at the default
`"lambda.1se"`, and the lasso scores [0.608]{.lang-r-only}[0.727]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[2]"}. The looser tolerance gives [the same AUC as the default to
three decimals]{.lang-r-only}[0.727]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[3]"}[ against ]{.lang-py-only}[0.729]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[0]"}[ at the default]{.lang-py-only}, and the timings at the end of the article show what it saves.
`maxent(classes = "lq")` scores [0.693]{.lang-r-only}[0.736]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[9]"} against [0.665]{.lang-r-only}[0.710]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[8]"} for the classes maxnet chooses, and both forests
score [close to 0.5]{.lang-r-only}[0.626]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[4]"}[ and ]{.lang-py-only}[0.605]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[5]"} at this grain on 75 units. A single split of 75 units is a noisy comparison, so a
difference of this size is worth checking under `timesift()`'s folds, with the two settings as two
named candidates, before acting on it.

## Neural encoders

The neural-network constructors `mlp()`, `cnn()` and `rescnn()` set the network structure, including layer widths and the number of neighbouring bins each convolution uses. `train_control()` sets how the networks are trained: passes through the data (epochs), observations per update (batch size), learning rate, optimiser, stopping rule and computing device. Settings on an individual learner override the corresponding settings for the run.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r control, eval = has_torch}
train_control(epochs = 5L, device = "cpu")
cnn(channels = c(8L, 16L), kernel = 3L, epochs = 10L)
```

```python
ts.train_control(epochs=5, device="cpu")
#> <timesift control>
#>   epochs           5
#>   batch_size       64   (default)
#>   learning_rate    0.001   (default)
#>   weight_decay     0.0001   (default)
#>   optimizer        adamw   (default)
#>   penalty          0.0   (default)
#>   alpha            0.5   (default)
#>   schedule         cosine   (default)
#>   plateau_factor   0.1   (default)
#>   plateau_patience 10   (default)
#>   early_stopping   inf   (default)
#>   val_frac         0.0   (default)
#>   device           cpu
#>   seed             1   (default)
#>   swa              False   (default)
#>   swa_start        0.7   (default)
ts.cnn(channels=(8, 16), kernel=3, epochs=10)
#> <timesift learner> cnn
#> reads   : sequence ; one model per response: no, joint
#> data    : every representation of the run
#> settings: channels = 8/16, kernel = 3, dropout = 0.3
#> training: epochs = 10
#> needs   : torch
```
:::

The control marks the settings that were not named as `(default)`, and the learner lists under
`training` the one setting it overrides. The run below trains both encoders at the weekly grain for
a handful of epochs on the processor. The run's control sets five epochs and the convolutional
encoder overrides it with ten. This keeps the example quick and leaves both networks undertrained.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r encoders, eval = has_torch}
nets <- timesift(targets, sim$readings, y = starts_with("v"), id = unit, time = time,
                 learners = c(mlp(hidden = c(32L, 16L)),
                              cnn(channels = c(8L, 16L), kernel = 3L, epochs = 10L)),
                 sift = grains("week"), control = train_control(epochs = 5L, device = "cpu"),
                 resampling = cv(v = 3), n_inner = NULL, ensemble = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
summary(nets)
```

```python
nets = ts.timesift(targets, sim.readings, y="v*", id="unit", time="time",
                   learners=[ts.mlp(hidden=(32, 16)), ts.cnn(channels=(8, 16), kernel=3, epochs=10)],
                   sift=ts.grains("week"), control=ts.train_control(epochs=5, device="cpu"),
                   resampling=ts.cv(v=3), n_inner=None, ensemble=False, verbose=False)
print(ts.summary(nets))
#> timesift  150 targets, 4 responses, 3-fold random CV, roc_auc
#>
#> candidates, scored on the outer folds
#> candidate            mean    won  responses
#> cnn / week          0.446      1  joint
#> mlp / week          0.463      3  joint
#>
#> choice on every target  mlp / week
```
:::

After so few epochs both encoders score close to 0.5, as an undertrained network does. The
`responses` column reads `joint`: one network covers all four responses, and each candidate is still
reported once.

A sequence learner pinned to a representation that gives one row of features is refused before the
record is read:

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r refuse-sequence, error = TRUE, eval = has_torch}
timesift(targets, sim$readings, y = starts_with("v"), id = unit, time = time,
         learners = cnn(data = multigrain(c("week", "month"))), verbose = FALSE)
```

```{.python error=true}
ts.timesift(targets, sim.readings, y="v*", id="unit", time="time",
            learners=ts.cnn(data=ts.multigrain(("week", "month"))), verbose=False)
#> ValueError: no learner can read any of the representations:
#>   cnn() reads a sequence; multigrain(week+month) gives one row of 65 features
```
:::

A fitted encoder holds its weights as plain arrays and the device as the setting it was given, so a
fit saved with `saveRDS()` on a machine with a graphics card predicts after `readRDS()` on one
without.

## Tuning

`tune()` wraps a learner so that, each time it is fitted, it cross-validates a grid of its own
settings on the units it is handed and fits the setting that scored best. In a run each outer fold
tunes on its own training units, so the setting a fold is scored with was never chosen on that
fold's held-out units. A grid names settings the learner carries, and every combination is tried.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r tune}
tuned <- tune(forest(trees = 200L), list(mtry = c(2L, 8L), min_node = c(1L, 5L)), n_inner = 3L)
tf <- fit_learner(tuned, week_train, sim$y[train, ])
tf$model$chosen
tf$model$table
```

```python
tuned = ts.tune(ts.forest(trees=200), {"mtry": (2, 8), "min_node": (1, 5)}, n_inner=3)
tf = ts.fit_learner(tuned, week_train, train)
tf.model.chosen
#> {'mtry': 8, 'min_node': 5}
pd.DataFrame(tf.model.table)
#>                  settings     score
#> 0  mtry = 2, min_node = 1  0.530352
#> 1  mtry = 8, min_node = 1  0.553803
#> 2  mtry = 2, min_node = 5  0.520598
#> 3  mtry = 8, min_node = 5  0.566769
```
:::

The search chose [`mtry = 8` and `min_node = 5`]{.lang-r-only}[`mtry = 8` and `min_node = 5`]{.lang-py-only py="'`mtry = %d` and `min_node = %d`' % (tf.model.chosen['mtry'], tf.model.chosen['min_node'])"}, the combination with the highest mean inner AUC.
Under `timesift()`, the settings each tuned candidate chose on all targets are in the `settings`
column of the candidate table.

Given no `grid`, `tune()` searches the grid registered under the learner's name. Eight shipped
learners carry the grids that biomod2's `BIOMOD_Tuning()` searches:

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r tunings}
tunings()
```

```python
ts.tunings()
#> ['boosting', 'discriminant', 'envelope', 'forest', 'mars', 'maxent', 'mlp', 'perceptron']
```
:::

`register_tuning()` adds a grid, as a named list or as a function of the learner and the array for a
grid that depends on the data, such as one bounded by the number of columns. The elastic net has no
grid registered; the one below searches its mixing.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r register-tuning}
register_tuning("elasticnet", list(alpha = c(0.25, 1)))
te <- fit_learner(tune(elasticnet(), n_inner = 3L), month_train, sim$y[train, ])
te$model$table
```

```python
ts.register_tuning("elasticnet", {"alpha": (0.25, 1)});
te = ts.fit_learner(ts.tune(ts.elasticnet(), n_inner=3), month_train, train)
pd.DataFrame(te.model.table)
#>        settings     score
#> 0  alpha = 0.25  0.578892
#> 1     alpha = 1  0.598877
```
:::

`alpha = 1`, the lasso, scored higher on the three inner folds, and the tuned learner was fitted
with it. The registration lasts for the session, and replacing a grid already registered takes
`overwrite = TRUE`.

## A learner of one's own

`learner()` takes a `fit` and a `predict` function, and `fit` is handed what it declares. A `fit`
with an argument called `weights` receives the response head's case weights, one per cell of the
response. One with `head` receives the head itself, whose `loss` says what to fit toward. One with
`control` receives the resolved `train_control()`, and one with `group` receives the grouping the
outer folds keep whole, so that a split drawn inside the fit keeps it too. A `fit` that declares
none of these is fitted unweighted, with nothing but the array and the response.

The learner below reduces every channel to its mean over the bins and fits one generalised linear
model per response, in the family the head's loss names.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r own}
channel_means <- function(data = NULL) {
  learner(
    "channel_means",
    fit = function(x, y, head, weights, ...) {
      f <- data.frame(apply(unclass(x), c(1L, 3L), mean))
      family <- switch(head$loss,
                       binary_cross_entropy = stats::quasibinomial(),
                       squared_error = stats::gaussian(),
                       poisson_deviance = stats::quasipoisson())
      lapply(seq_len(ncol(y)), function(j) {
        stats::glm(y[, j] ~ ., data = f, weights = weights[, j], family = family)
      })
    },
    predict = function(model, x) {
      f <- data.frame(apply(unclass(x), c(1L, 3L), mean))
      vapply(model, function(m) stats::predict(m, f, type = "response"), numeric(nrow(f)))
    },
    data = data
  )
}
channel_means()
```

```python
families = {
    "binary_cross_entropy": (lambda eta: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-eta)), lambda mu: mu * (1 - mu)),
    "squared_error": (lambda eta: eta, np.ones_like),
    "poisson_deviance": (np.exp, lambda mu: mu),
}

def glm(design, y, w, loss):
    inverse, variance = families[loss]
    beta = np.zeros(design.shape[1])
    for _ in range(50):
        mu = inverse(design @ beta)
        step = np.linalg.solve(design.T @ ((w * variance(mu))[:, None] * design),
                               design.T @ (w * (y - mu)))
        beta += step
        if np.abs(step).max() < 1e-8:
            break
    return beta

def channel_means(data=None):
    def design(x):
        return np.column_stack([np.ones(x.values.shape[0]), x.values.mean(axis=1)])

    def fit(x, y, head, weights, **_):
        return [glm(design(x), y[:, j], weights[:, j], head["loss"]) for j in range(y.shape[1])], head

    def predict(model, x):
        betas, head = model
        inverse = families[head["loss"]][0]
        return np.column_stack([inverse(design(x) @ b) for b in betas])

    return ts.Learner("channel_means", fit=fit, predict=predict, data=data)

channel_means()
#> <timesift learner> channel_means
#> reads   : tabular ; one model per response: yes, separate
#> data    : every representation of the run
```
:::

`register_learner()` makes the constructor available by name, beside the shipped learners, and a
registered learner can then be given to `timesift()` or `fit_learner()` as its name alone. A fit made
by a registered learner is saved as the learner's name and settings, so a session that reads the fit
back with `readRDS()` registers the learner again before predicting from it.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r register-learner}
register_learner("channel_means", channel_means)
"channel_means" %in% learners()
own <- timesift(targets, sim$readings, y = starts_with("v"), id = unit, time = time,
                learners = c(elasticnet(), channel_means()),
                sift = grains("week", "month"),
                resampling = cv(v = 5), n_inner = NULL, ensemble = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
summary(own)
```

```python
ts.register_learner("channel_means", channel_means);
"channel_means" in ts.learners()
#> True
own = ts.timesift(targets, sim.readings, y="v*", id="unit", time="time",
                  learners=[ts.elasticnet(), channel_means()],
                  sift=ts.grains("week", "month"),
                  resampling=ts.cv(v=5), n_inner=None, ensemble=False, verbose=False)
print(ts.summary(own))
#> timesift  150 targets, 4 responses, 5-fold random CV, roc_auc
#>
#> candidates, scored on the outer folds
#> candidate                       mean    won  responses
#> channel_means / month          0.470      0  separate
#> channel_means / week           0.472      0  separate
#> elasticnet / month             0.571      0  separate
#> elasticnet / week              0.789      4  separate
#>
#> choice on every target  elasticnet / week
```
:::

`channel_means` scores [0.461 at both grains]{.lang-r-only}[0.470 at the monthly grain and 0.472 at the weekly]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f at the monthly grain and %.3f at the weekly' % ({r['candidate']: r['mean'] for r in ts.candidate_table(own)}['channel_means / month'], {r['candidate']: r['mean'] for r in ts.candidate_table(own)}['channel_means / week'])"}. The mean of a channel over the whole year is nearly
the same number whichever bins it is averaged from, and in this simulation the responses read each
unit's departure from its own level, which a yearly mean averages away. The weekly elastic net,
which reads every bin, scores [0.701]{.lang-r-only}[0.789]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % {r['candidate']: r['mean'] for r in ts.candidate_table(own)}['elasticnet / week']"}.

## Other responses, and other metrics

A response head defines the response type, fitting loss and conditions under which a cell can be scored. In addition to `"presence_absence"`, four response heads are available:

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r responses}
responses()
```

```python
ts.responses()
#> ['abundance', 'continuous', 'count', 'ordinal', 'presence_absence']
```
:::

A count is fitted under the Poisson deviance. The counts below are drawn from each unit's mean
reading, and the forest fits them with no change to the learner.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r counts}
week <- grain_matrix(sim$readings, unit, time, reading, grain = "week")
rate <- exp(0.5 + 0.8 * as.numeric(scale(apply(week, 1L, mean))))
counts <- matrix(rpois(150, rate), ncol = 1L, dimnames = list(rownames(sim$y), "count"))
cf <- fit_learner(forest(), week_train, counts[train, , drop = FALSE], response = "count")
round(head(predict(cf, week_test), 3), 2)
```

```python
week = ts.grain_matrix(sim.readings, "unit", "time", "reading", grain="week")
level = week.values.mean(axis=(1, 2))
rate = np.exp(0.5 + 0.8 * (level - level.mean()) / level.std(ddof=1))
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
counts = ts.Response(rng.poisson(rate).reshape(-1, 1).astype(float), y.units, ("count",))
counts_train = counts.take_units(np.arange(75))
cf = ts.fit_learner(ts.forest(), week_train, counts_train, response="count")
cf.predict(week_test)[:3].round(2)
#> array([[0.65],
#>        [2.66],
#>        [1.43]])
```
:::

`maxent()`, `envelope()`, `discriminant()` and `hierarchical()` need a presence-absence response and
refuse any other head:

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r counts-refuse, error = TRUE}
fit_learner(maxent(), week_train, counts[train, , drop = FALSE], response = "count")
```

```{.python error=true}
ts.fit_learner(ts.maxent(), week_train, counts_train, response="count")
#> ValueError: maxnet fits a presence-absence response, under a head whose loss is the binary cross-entropy; this head's loss is 'poisson_deviance'.
```
:::

`register_response()` adds a head. Its specification names `prepare`, `activation`, `loss`,
`metric` and `cells`, and optionally `weights`. The activation and the loss are each one of the
three the learners know: `"sigmoid"`, `"identity"` or `"exp"`, and `"binary_cross_entropy"`,
`"squared_error"` or `"poisson_deviance"`. The shipped presence-absence head weights each presence
by the ratio of absences to presences among the fitting units, capped at 50 by default, through
`positive_weights()`. The weight of a presence in each response of this record:

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r weights}
w <- positive_weights(sim$y)
apply(w, 2L, max)
```

```python
w = ts.positive_weights(y)
w.max(axis=0)
#> array([2.125     , 2.        , 2.40909091, 2.125     ])
```
:::

A head with a different cap reaches every learner through one registration. With a cap of 2, the
presences of `v01` and `v03` weigh 2 and those of `v02` and `v04` keep the weights above.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r register-response}
register_response("presence_absence_cap2", list(
  prepare = function(y) {
    y <- as.matrix(y)
    storage.mode(y) <- "double"
    if (!all(y %in% c(0, 1))) stop("a presence-absence response is 0/1.", call. = FALSE)
    y
  },
  activation = "sigmoid",
  loss = "binary_cross_entropy",
  metric = "roc_auc",
  cells = function(y, folds) scorable_cells(y, folds),
  weights = function(y, fitting) positive_weights(y, cap = 2, fitting = fitting)
))
```

```python
ts.register_response("presence_absence_cap2", {
    "prepare": lambda y: ts.as_response(y).check_presence_absence(),
    "activation": "sigmoid",
    "loss": "binary_cross_entropy",
    "metric": "roc_auc",
    "cells": lambda y, folds: ts.scorable_cells(y, folds),
    "weights": lambda y, fitting: ts.positive_weights(y, cap=2, fitting=fitting),
});
```
:::

A metric is a function of the observed values and the predictions of one held-out cell.
`register_metric()` adds one by name, and `timesift(metric = )` then chooses and reports by it. The
Brier score below has its sign reversed, so that a higher score is better, as the choice of a
candidate assumes of every metric.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r register-metric}
register_metric("neg_brier", function(y, p) -mean((y - p)^2))
capped <- timesift(targets, sim$readings, y = starts_with("v"), id = unit, time = time,
                   learners = c(elasticnet(), forest()), sift = grains("month"),
                   response = "presence_absence_cap2", metric = "neg_brier",
                   resampling = cv(v = 5), n_inner = NULL, ensemble = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
summary(capped)
```

```python
ts.register_metric("neg_brier", lambda y, p: -np.mean((y - p) ** 2));
capped = ts.timesift(targets, sim.readings, y="v*", id="unit", time="time",
                     learners=[ts.elasticnet(), ts.forest()], sift=ts.grains("month"),
                     response="presence_absence_cap2", metric="neg_brier",
                     resampling=ts.cv(v=5), n_inner=None, ensemble=False, verbose=False)
print(ts.summary(capped))
#> timesift  150 targets, 4 responses, 5-fold random CV, neg_brier
#>
#> candidates, scored on the outer folds
#> candidate                    mean    won  responses
#> forest / month             -0.240      2  separate
#> elasticnet / month         -0.238      2  separate
#>
#> choice on every target  elasticnet / month
```
:::

The run is chosen and reported by the Brier score under the capped weights. The elastic net, at
[-0.239]{.lang-r-only}[-0.238]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % {r['candidate']: r['mean'] for r in ts.candidate_table(capped)}['elasticnet / month']"}, scored above the forest, at [-0.259]{.lang-r-only}[-0.240]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % {r['candidate']: r['mean'] for r in ts.candidate_table(capped)}['forest / month']"}, and scored highest on [all four]{.lang-r-only}[2 of the four]{.lang-py-only py="str({r['candidate']: r['won'] for r in ts.candidate_table(capped)}['elasticnet / month']) + ' of the four'"} responses.

## Choosing learners

The cost of a learner depends on how many columns its representation flattens to, and on how much
of its fit is an inner search. The timings below fit each tabular learner once on all 150 units and
four responses at the weekly grain, which flattens to 53 columns.

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r timings}
timed <- list(elasticnet = elasticnet(), `elasticnet(tol = 1e-4)` = elasticnet(tol = 1e-4),
              linear = linear(), tree = tree(), forest = forest(), boosting = boosting(),
              xgboost = boosting(method = "xgboost"), maxent = maxent(),
              envelope = envelope(), mars = mars(), discriminant = discriminant(),
              perceptron = perceptron(), hierarchical = hierarchical())
seconds <- vapply(timed, function(l) {
  system.time(fit_learner(l, week, sim$y))[["elapsed"]]
}, numeric(1))
sort(round(seconds, 2), decreasing = TRUE)
```

```python
timed = {
    "elasticnet": ts.elasticnet(), "elasticnet(tol=1e-4)": ts.elasticnet(tol=1e-4),
    "linear": ts.linear(), "tree": ts.tree(), "forest": ts.forest(), "boosting": ts.boosting(),
    "xgboost": ts.boosting(method="xgboost"), "maxent": ts.maxent(),
    "envelope": ts.envelope(), "mars": ts.mars(), "discriminant": ts.discriminant(),
    "perceptron": ts.perceptron(), "hierarchical": ts.hierarchical(),
}

def seconds_to_fit(learner, x=week):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    ts.fit_learner(learner, x, y)
    return time.perf_counter() - start

seconds = pd.Series({name: seconds_to_fit(l) for name, l in timed.items()})
seconds.round(2).sort_values(ascending=False)
#> linear                  4.95
#> elasticnet              3.78
#> maxent                  0.51
#> forest                  0.47
#> elasticnet(tol=1e-4)    0.17
#> discriminant            0.17
#> xgboost                 0.09
#> perceptron              0.03
#> boosting                0.03
#> tree                    0.02
#> mars                    0.01
#> hierarchical            0.01
#> envelope                0.00
#> dtype: float64
```
:::

`additive()` is not in that list, because at its default `k = 10` an additive model of 53 columns
needs more coefficients than there are units:

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r additive-refuse, error = TRUE}
fit_learner(additive(), week, sim$y)
```

```{.python error=true}
ts.fit_learner(ts.additive(), week, y)
#> ValueError: an additive model of 478 coefficients has more than the 150 units it is fitted to; fewer columns or a smaller `k` fit.
```
:::

At the monthly grain, 12 columns, it fits, and its cost depends on `k`:

::: {.lang-pair}
```{r additive-month}
month <- grain_matrix(sim$readings, unit, time, reading, grain = "month")
additive_seconds <- c(
  `k = 10` = system.time(fit_learner(additive(), month, sim$y))[["elapsed"]],
  `k = 5` = system.time(fit_learner(additive(k = 5L), month, sim$y))[["elapsed"]])
round(additive_seconds, 2)
```

```python
month = ts.grain_matrix(sim.readings, "unit", "time", "reading", grain="month")
additive_seconds = pd.Series({"k = 10": seconds_to_fit(ts.additive(), month),
                              "k = 5": seconds_to_fit(ts.additive(k=5), month)})
additive_seconds.round(2)
#> k = 10    12.13
#> k = 5      0.68
#> dtype: float64
```
:::

With `k = 10` the fit took [`r round(additive_seconds[["k = 10"]], 1)`]{.lang-r-only}[12.1]{.lang-py-only py="format(additive_seconds['k = 10'], '.1f')"} seconds, and with `k = 5` it
took [`r round(additive_seconds[["k = 5"]], 1)`]{.lang-r-only}[0.7]{.lang-py-only py="format(additive_seconds['k = 5'], '.1f')"} seconds.

The elastic net includes every predictor and uses a penalty to limit coefficient size. It chooses that penalty within the training data. At its default tolerance it took [`r round(seconds[["elasticnet"]], 1)`]{.lang-r-only}[3.8]{.lang-py-only py="format(seconds['elasticnet'], '.1f')"} seconds here; `tol = 1e-4` took [`r round(seconds[["elasticnet(tol = 1e-4)"]], 1)`]{.lang-r-only}[0.2]{.lang-py-only py="format(seconds['elasticnet(tol=1e-4)'], '.1f')"} seconds and gave [the same held-out AUC on the split above]{.lang-r-only}[a held-out AUC of ]{.lang-py-only}[0.727]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[3]"}[ on the split above, against ]{.lang-py-only}[0.729]{.lang-py-only py="'%.3f' % held_out.iloc[0]"}[ at the default]{.lang-py-only}. `linear()` took [`r round(seconds[["linear"]], 1)`]{.lang-r-only}[4.9]{.lang-py-only py="format(seconds['linear'], '.1f')"} seconds. Its search refits the model for each term it could add or remove, with 106 possible terms at the weekly grain. A coarser grain or a bounded search, such as `linear(select = "forward", terms = "column", max_terms = 3)`, reduces the number of fits. Every other tabular learner took at most [`r round(max(seconds[!names(seconds) %in% c("linear", "elasticnet")]), 2)`]{.lang-r-only}[0.51]{.lang-py-only py="format(seconds.drop(['linear', 'elasticnet']).max(), '.2f')"} seconds.

What a learner can be fitted on depends on the number of units against the number of columns its
representation flattens to:

- The additive model holds one coefficient for the intercept and `k - 1` for each column, and
  refuses a fit with more coefficients than units. On a small sample it needs a coarse grain or a
  small `k`, and its cost grows with `k`, as the timings above show.
- `linear(select = "none")` fits every term without selecting, and over more columns than units it
  separates any response it is given. It is meant for a coarse grain such as
  `data = grain("season")`.
- The envelope keeps a unit inside only where every column agrees, so each added column leaves
  fewer presences inside. It too is meant for a coarse grain.
- The elastic net, the forest and boosting keep a wide block fittable on few units through the
  penalty, the column draw and the shrinkage, which makes them the first learners to run at a fine
  grain on a small sample.
- `maxent()` builds a hinge per column per knot, so its design grows with the grain. A fit whose
  design would pass `max_design` gigabytes is refused with the size it would have taken, and a
  coarser grain or fewer classes brings it within the limit.
- `perceptron()` reads the columns in their own units unless `standardise = TRUE`, and a record in
  degrees saturates its hidden units sooner the wider its range.

The encoders fit every response through one network, so a rarer response borrows from the common
ones. That pooling is what they are for, and it needs many responses and enough units to train a
network on. In the Schrankogel study, 894 plots and 101 species read hourly for three years, a fully
connected network on the series was level with a penalised logistic model on 188 hand-built
features, and the gain came from convolution reading the series at a coarse grain. A study with few
units and few responses may gain little from the encoders over the elastic net, and pays for the
training.

A learner is the wrong choice where it cannot read the response or the representation. `maxent()`,
`envelope()`, `discriminant()` and `hierarchical()` fit presence-absence alone. A tabular learner
cannot read `native()`, and a sequence learner cannot read a `multigrain()` block or a
representation of one bin. A learner can also be handed a reduction that has already discarded the
signal: `channel_means` above was fitted correctly and scored below 0.5, because a yearly mean keeps
nothing of a weekly departure. No learner recovers what the representation dropped, which is why
`timesift()` compares learners across grains.
